questions.question: How does MySQL primary-replica replication work and how does it affect a Spring Boot application's read/write strategy?
questions.title: MySQL Replication: Primary-Replica Setup
questions.direct_answer: MySQL replication streams binary log (binlog) events from the primary to one or more replicas asynchronously. The replica's I/O thread fetches binlog events, and the SQL thread replays them. In Spring Boot, you configure separate DataSource beans for reads (replica) and writes (primary) using AbstractRoutingDataSource to distribute load and scale reads horizontally.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests architecture awareness and ability to design scalable database layers. Interviewers want to see that the candidate understands replication lag, read-after-write consistency risks, and how to handle them in Spring Boot.

sections.title: How MySQL Replication Scales Reads
sections.content: MySQL replication allows one primary (master) node to replicate all writes to one or more replica (slave) nodes. The primary writes changes to its binary log; each replica connects, downloads binlog events, and applies them in sequence. This enables read scaling (route SELECT queries to replicas), high availability (replica can be promoted if primary fails), and backups without impacting the primary. The critical gotcha is replication lag: replicas may be seconds behind the primary, causing stale reads after a write.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Async replication allows data loss on primary crash** — the primary commits and acknowledges before any replica confirms receipt; semi-sync replication eliminates this window at the cost of write latency
- **Replication lag breaks read-your-writes** — a user reads from a lagging replica immediately after writing and sees the old value; route reads to the primary for a short post-write window to guarantee consistency
- **Row-based replication (binlog_format=ROW) is safer than statement-based** — replicates exact row changes; statement-based replication breaks for non-deterministic functions like `NOW()` or `RAND()`
- **`SHOW REPLICA STATUS`** — shows `Seconds_Behind_Source` (replica lag) and any SQL/IO thread errors; the first monitoring check for replication problems
- **GTID-based replication simplifies failover** — Global Transaction IDs make it possible to promote any replica to primary without manually calculating binlog position; strongly recommended for new setups

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
MySQL primary-replica replication is the standard way to scale reads — the primary handles all writes and streams those changes to one or more replicas via the binary log.

**How it works**
- Every write on the primary is recorded in the binary log (binlog) in the order it commits — each replica runs an I/O thread that connects to the primary and copies the binlog, then an SQL thread that replays those events on the replica's local data
- The replica applies events asynchronously by default, which means there's always some replication lag — how much depends on the replica's hardware and how fast the primary is generating writes

**Asynchronous vs semi-synchronous replication**
- With default async replication, a primary acknowledges a commit before any replica confirms receipt — which means a primary crash can lose committed transactions that hadn't yet been streamed to replicas
- Semi-synchronous replication (`rpl_semi_sync_master_enabled`) waits for at least one replica to acknowledge receiving the binlog before the primary acknowledges the commit — this reduces the data loss window at the cost of slightly higher write latency

**Replication lag and read-your-writes**
- Replication lag means a read replica may return stale data — a user who just submitted a form may not see their change on the next page load if the read goes to a lagging replica
- The Spring Boot solution: use `@Primary` or a separate DataSource for writes, and route reads to replicas; implement read-your-writes by routing reads to the primary for a short window after a write, or using `WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET` to wait for the replica to catch up

Row-based replication (binlog_format=ROW) replicates the exact row changes rather than the SQL statements, which makes replication deterministic for non-deterministic functions like `NOW()` and avoids many replication consistency issues.
